what_its_for: Nifedipine is used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and chest pain (angina). It belongs to a group of medicines called calcium channel blockers. It works by relaxing and widening your blood vessels, which makes it easier for your heart to pump blood and lowers your blood pressure.
how_to_take: Take nifedipine exactly as your doctor prescribed. Swallow extended-release tablets (the long-acting kind, often labeled XL or CC) whole — do not crush, chew, or break them. You may take the regular capsules with or without food, but take extended-release tablets on an empty stomach or with a light meal. Try to take it at the same time each day to keep your levels steady.
dosing: Your doctor will set the right dose for you. The usual starting dose for adults is 30 mg to 60 mg once daily for extended-release tablets, or 10 mg three times a day for immediate-release capsules. Your doctor may adjust your dose based on how your body responds. Never change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next scheduled dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store nifedipine at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep it in its original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of unused or expired medicine safely — ask your pharmacist about a drug take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking grapefruit juice or eating grapefruit while taking nifedipine. Grapefruit can cause more of the medicine to enter your bloodstream, which may increase your risk of side effects. Avoid rising too quickly from a sitting or lying position, as nifedipine can cause dizziness or lightheadedness, especially at first. Limit alcohol, as it can lower your blood pressure further and increase dizziness. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: severe chest pain or worsening angina, very fast or irregular heartbeat, shortness of breath, severe dizziness or fainting, sudden swelling of your hands, feet, or ankles, yellowing of your skin or eyes (signs of liver problems), or signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also call your doctor if your blood pressure readings remain high or if you feel the medicine is not working.
when_it_works: For high blood pressure, nifedipine starts to lower your blood pressure within a few hours of your first dose, but it may take 1 to 2 weeks of regular use to see the full benefit. For chest pain (angina), you may notice fewer episodes relatively quickly. Keep taking the medicine even if you feel well — high blood pressure often has no symptoms, and stopping suddenly can be dangerous.
special_populations: Older adults (over 65): You may be more sensitive to the blood pressure-lowering effects of nifedipine. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose and increase it slowly. Be extra careful about dizziness and falling. Pregnancy: Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Nifedipine is sometimes used during pregnancy under close medical supervision, but your doctor needs to weigh the risks and benefits. Breastfeeding: Small amounts of nifedipine can pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you have kidney or liver disease, as your body may process this medicine differently.
